newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to stay in hospital, Lebed visits Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to stay in hospital, Lebed visits Chechnya.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin looked relaxed in television pictures filmed on Tuesday but a spokesman said he was likely to stay in hospital for the rest of this week to prepare for heart surgery.
Yeltsin was filmed holding talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on problems including breakaway Chechnya and a strike by about 10,000 power workers in Russia's far east.

Security tsar Alexander Lebed flew to Chechnya to tackle the first problem. He met separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev to try to shore up a peace deal and pledged that Moscow would push on with a troop withdrawal which was suspended last week.
The governor of the far eastern region of Primorsky Krai held out hope that the strike there would be resolved soon, but gave no details of a planned deal which he hoped would end it.
Yeltsin, 65, smiled and gesticulated with his hands during brief, silent footage of his talks with Chernomyrdin filmed by Russia Television.

But presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin would remain for more tests in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital, where he has been since Friday. His stay appears to be longer than first planned.
"It is very likely that Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) will stay in the Central Clinical Hospital until the end of the week," Yastrzhembsky told a Kremlin briefing.
"He is in hospital, to the delight of the doctors who have at last got their hands on him as an in-patient."

Yastrzhembsky said a council of doctors would decide on September 25 or 26 when to operate on the president. Yeltsin, who had two heart attacks last year, is expected to have a bypass operation to increase the flow of blood to his heart.

In response to media speculation that Yeltsin has felt worse and depressed since he announced on September 5 that he would have surgery, Yastrzhembsky said the meeting with Chernomyrdin would not have taken place if the reports were true.
Yastrzhembsky gave no details of any plans for Yeltsin to hand over his duties while he has surgery or who would have the "red button" controlling Russia's nuclear weapons.
Lebed, Yeltsin's envoy to Chehcnya, met Yandarbiyev and rebel commander Aslan Maskhadov to try to consolidate a peace deal signed on August 31.
He sounded confident after the talks in Novye Atagi, 20 km (12 miles) south of the Chechen capital Grozny.
"We are continuing to move towards a durable, long and perhaps everlasting peace," Lebed told reporters.
The deal, including a five-year deferral of the question of Chechnya's future status and the troop pullout, is intended to halt a 21-month-old conflict which has killed tens of thousands.
But some officials in Moscow have distanced themselves from the deal and Moscow's top commander in the region suspended the pullout last week to press for an exchange of prisoners.

Lebed said the withdrawal would continue and that he and Yandarbiyev had agreed in principle on the formation of a coalition government in Chechnya -- one of the potential sticking points. He gave no details.
Power workers went on strike this week in Primorsky Krai to demand months of unpaid wages. They have blocked out parts of the region of more than two million people on the Pacific coast.

Regional governor Yevgeny Nazdratenko told reporters he was about to sign a deal to help solve mutual debts and end the crisis fast. He gave no details and critics say the problems may be too complex to settle immediately.
